塔馬變音鼓屬膜鳴樂器，霍恩博斯特爾—薩克斯編號211.242.11，為西非沙漏形: The tama is a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.242.11, a West African hourglass-shaped two-headed drum whose pitch is changed by the tension of leather cords and which is played held under the arm. It can be used to send messages, and it has entered West African popular music such as mbalax in Senegal and fuji and jùjú in Nigeria; it appears at weddings, funerals and private ceremonies and in African ensembles. In the Serer “wune / shat” tradition of Senegal and Gambia the tama is the fourth drum of the ensemble, played together with the pëngël, the lambe and the jinë.
塔馬變音鼓屬西非沙漏形膜鳴樂器，歷史可追溯至博諾人、約魯巴人、迦納帝國與豪薩人。: The tama is a West African hourglass-shaped membranophone whose history can be traced to the Bono, the Yoruba, the Ghana Empire and the Hausa. From the eighteenth century drummers sent ceremonial messages and commands by pitch and rhythm, over distances of four to five miles. The Serer of Senegal and Gambia also use the tama in the dance tradition held before boys' circumcision, where it has religious meaning. In the twentieth century the drum entered West African popular music, in mbalax, fuji and jùjú, and it continues at weddings, funerals and in ensembles.
塔馬變音鼓是西非沙漏形膜鳴鼓，屬霍恩博斯特尔—薩克斯分類211.242.11。它: The tama is a West African hourglass-shaped membranophone drum, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.242.11. It has two heads joined by leather cords; the player holds it under the arm and changes the pitch by squeezing or releasing the cords with the arm, imitating the tones and rhythms of speech. The Serer use it in the “won” tradition and in the dance before circumcision, which has religious meaning; griots also beat it on special occasions such as war or the summoning of subjects.
塔馬變音鼓為膜鳴樂器，兩面鼓皮以皮繩相連，演奏者夾於腋下，以手臂與身體擠壓或放鬆: The tama is a membranophone; its two heads are joined by leather cords, and the player holds it under the arm and squeezes or releases the cords with arm and body, changing the tension of the heads so that the pitch slides up or down within a single stroke, producing a vibrato like a humming voice. The source does not say how the volume is controlled, but the drum can reproduce the pitch, loudness and rhythm of human speech, though not vowels and consonants. Similar hourglass drums in Asia are mostly not used to imitate conversation; the idakka, on the other hand, is used to imitate singing.
塔馬變音鼓為西非沙漏形膜鳴樂器，演奏時將鼓身夾於腋下，使鼓腰貼近手臂與肋骨。鼓面: The tama is a West African hourglass-shaped membranophone; it is played held under the arm, with the waist of the drum against the arm and the ribs. The heads are joined by leather tension cords; a beginner first squeezes or releases the cords with the arm to change the tension of the heads, and then strikes the head to sound it. Squeezing raises the pitch and releasing lowers it, and a slide can be made within a single stroke. The point is not to imitate vowels or consonants but to master tone, loudness and rhythm. When learning drum speech, each word goes with a fixed phrase; a beginner should first memorise these matching phrases, then practise continuous striking and pauses.
塔馬變音鼓鼓體由當地工匠以硬木材製作，如非洲紅木等，經精心雕刻成圓筒形。鼓面採用: The body of the tama is made by local craftsmen from hardwoods such as African mahogany, carefully carved into a cylindrical shape. The heads are of natural animal skin, usually goatskin or cowhide, which resonates well. The sides carry a tension system of natural hemp or leather cord that adjusts how tight the heads are. Some modern versions use synthetic leather and nylon cord for durability and stability, but traditional handmade drums still use natural materials.
